questions.prompt: Why does an optimizer need each plan node's output cardinality?
options: Output cardinality always equals the operator's I/O count
It becomes an input-size estimate for costing parent operators
The root's output count alone determines every input size
Every parent preserves its child's row count
questions.explanation: Downstream work depends on intermediate results. A small final output does not imply that all preceding steps are cheap.

questions.prompt: What does a System R-style cost model, I/O + CPU-factor×tuples, combine?
options: Only directly measured wall-clock time
Only the number of index levels
Disk access and estimated tuple-processing work
Only the number of output pages
questions.explanation: This is a weighted cost model, not an exact measurement of the eventual runtime.

questions.prompt: What can happen if a child's output is underestimated by a factor of 100?
options: Only the final output estimate changes; plan decisions are unaffected
The parent is guaranteed to do less work because the estimate is small
Nothing changes as long as the logical semantics are correct
The parent may choose a poor join or memory strategy because its expected input is too small
questions.explanation: Correct semantics do not guarantee accurate estimates. Cardinality errors propagate into parent costs and can change plan choices.

questions.prompt: Must two join plans with the same final cardinality have the same cost?
options: No; their intermediate sizes and algorithms can differ
Yes; cost depends only on the final row count
Yes; the same join predicate guarantees equal intermediate costs
They can differ only if DISTINCT is required
questions.explanation: The work performed before producing the final result can differ greatly. Final output size alone does not determine cost.

questions.prompt: Which pair of inputs matters when costing a physical operator?
options: Only the logical operator name, without its implementation
Input-size estimates and a cost formula appropriate to the implementation
Only the final SELECT column names
Only the cardinality of the largest table
questions.explanation: Hash, merge, and nested-loop implementations have different cost formulas. Each must be evaluated with the relevant input sizes.

questions.prompt: What does NKeys(A) represent in this model?
options: The number of bytes per A value
The number of pages in the index root
The number of distinct A values
The total number of rows, including duplicates
questions.explanation: Distinct-value count differs from tuple count. Confusing them gives an incorrect equality-selectivity estimate.

questions.prompt: A table has 10,000 tuples on 100 pages. Which statistic determines basic heap-scan I/O?
options: NTuples=10,000 treated as page reads
NKeys of the output column
Index height, even though no index is used
NPages=100
questions.explanation: A heap scan's I/O is measured in pages. It does not normally require a separate I/O for each tuple.

questions.prompt: Why is refreshing statistics useful after a bulk load changes the distribution?
options: Old estimates may no longer reflect the new cardinality or distribution
Refreshing automatically adds every needed index
Refreshing makes all values uniformly distributed
It repairs incorrect query semantics
questions.explanation: Statistics support planning. Refreshing them does not make the data uniform or create indexes.

questions.prompt: A selection produces 2,000 rows from 10,000 input rows. What is its selectivity?
questions.explanation: Selectivity=output/input=0.2. For a selection, this fraction lies between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase 'highly selective predicate' usually mean?
options: Its numerical selectivity is close to 1
It uses an index even though it retains most rows
It retains a small fraction of rows
It contains many conjuncts, regardless of combined selectivity
questions.explanation: The wording can be counterintuitive: a highly selective predicate usually has a small numerical selectivity s.

questions.prompt: A has 20 uniformly distributed distinct values, and c belongs to its domain. What is the estimate for sel(A=c)?
questions.explanation: 1/20=0.05. The distinct-value count is the denominator, not the selectivity itself.

questions.prompt: Integer A is uniform from 10 through 29, inclusive. What is sel(A>24)?
questions.explanation: The 5 values 25..29 qualify out of 20 possible values. Including both endpoints adds 1 when counting the domain.

questions.prompt: P has selectivity 0.2 and Q has selectivity 0.3. They are independent and have no NULLs. What is the selectivity of P AND Q?
questions.explanation: For independent predicates, AND multiplies 0.2 × 0.3. The value 0.44 is the OR estimate; 0.5 ignores the overlap.

questions.prompt: P and Q have selectivities 0.2 and 0.3, are independent, and have no NULLs. What is the selectivity of P OR Q?
questions.explanation: OR = 0.2 + 0.3 − 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.44. The value 0.5 double-counts the overlap; 0.06 is AND under independence.

questions.prompt: P has selectivity 0.15 and has no NULLs. What is the selectivity of NOT P?
questions.explanation: The complement is 1−0.15. NULLs would require SQL's three-valued logic, which the question explicitly excludes.

questions.prompt: S has 900 rows and a valid, non-null foreign key referencing R's unique key. How many rows does their inner join on that key produce?
options: Always |R|×900
Nothing can be inferred, even with the valid foreign key
questions.explanation: Each of the 900 S rows has a valid non-NULL reference, so a matching R row exists; uniqueness permits only one such match. Thus every S row contributes exactly one joined row: 900. Removing either assumption invalidates that exact count.

questions.prompt: With the same foreign key now nullable, 90 of S's 900 rows have NULL. All non-null references are valid. How many rows does the equality inner join return?
questions.explanation: NULL does not match using SQL equality. Each of the 810 non-null rows matches exactly one R row.

questions.prompt: Given |R|=600, |S|=900, V(R.a)=30, and V(S.a)=60, what is the equijoin-size estimate under uniformity and domain containment?
questions.explanation: 600 × 900/max(30,60)=9,000. Using the smaller distinct-value count would double this estimate.

questions.prompt: Is dividing by max(VR,VS) exact for every data distribution?
options: Yes, even when the domains are disjoint
Yes, as long as there are no NULLs
Yes, regardless of key skew
No; it relies on assumptions about uniformity and value overlap
questions.explanation: Disjoint domains can give 0 matches, while skew can greatly change the result. The formula is an estimate based on assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why does viewing a join as a selection over R×S help estimate its result size?
options: Start with candidate cardinality |R||S| and multiply by join selectivity
Every join must physically materialize R×S first
A join result cannot contain duplicates
Every join predicate has selectivity 1
questions.explanation: This is a logical way to derive a cardinality estimate. It does not require physically materializing the Cartesian product.

questions.prompt: What kind of information is a default selectivity used when statistics are missing?
options: A database constraint
A system fallback assumption
The actual measured frequency in that table
A guarantee from SQL semantics
questions.explanation: A default supports planning when information is missing. It is not a measurement of the table's actual distribution.

questions.prompt: Why should a default from PostgreSQL 13 not be treated as a universal constant across DBMSs and versions?
options: SQL prohibits fallback estimates
Every version has identical source code
Defaults depend on implementation and version
Selectivity never uses numerical values
questions.explanation: The slides illustrate a specific version. Its defaults are not a cross-system standard.

questions.prompt: A has 5 distinct values, but one value occurs in 80% of rows. What does a uniform equality estimate predict?
options: 80% automatically, because the distinct count is sufficient
100% for every equality
0%, because skew makes estimation impossible
20%, which is wrong for the hot value occurring in 80% of rows
questions.explanation: 1/5=20% assumes uniformity. The distinct-value count alone does not identify which value is frequent.

questions.prompt: What can reduce reliance on fallback estimates?
options: Collect or refresh appropriate statistics
Add DISTINCT to force a lower estimate, even though it changes the query
Force every predicate's selectivity to 1
Use the same old default for every column regardless of distribution changes
questions.explanation: Better statistics help the planner estimate the original query. Changing the query's meaning is not a valid way to repair an estimate.

questions.prompt: A default estimate predicts very few rows, but the actual row count is high. What can result?
options: The plan is guaranteed to return wrong answers
Many index probes or a join strategy that looked cheap may become expensive
The actual row count automatically falls to match the estimate
The equality predicate changes into a range
questions.explanation: Cardinality errors usually affect performance. They do not themselves change the logical query or its correct result.

questions.prompt: The integer domain 1..20 is divided into 4 equi-width buckets. What is each bucket's width?
questions.explanation: The inclusive domain contains 20 values, so the width is 20/4=5. Counting only 19 omits an endpoint.

questions.prompt: Bucket [6,10] contains 50 rows, uniformly distributed within the bucket. How many rows are estimated for A=8?
options: 50 rows
5 rows
25 rows
10 rows
questions.explanation: 50/5=10. The bucket total is shared among its values; it is not the frequency of every value.

questions.prompt: Buckets [1,5] and [6,10] contain 20 and 50 rows. Assuming uniformity within buckets, how many rows are estimated for A>8?
options: 20 rows
50 rows
30 rows
70 rows
questions.explanation: Only 9 and 10 qualify: 2/5 × 50=20. The strict > condition excludes 8.

questions.prompt: Using the same two buckets and uniformity assumption, how many rows are estimated for A>=4?
options: 54 rows
58 rows
70 rows
50 rows
questions.explanation: Values 4 and 5 contribute 2/5 × 20=8 rows. All 50 rows in bucket 6..10 qualify, giving 58 in total.

questions.prompt: What trade-off usually comes with adding histogram buckets?
options: Metadata always decreases while resolution improves
The actual table cardinality changes
Better resolution requires more metadata
Any single bucket always describes the exact distribution
questions.explanation: More buckets can reduce estimation error, but require more catalog space. They do not change the underlying data.

questions.prompt: Which quantity does an equi-depth histogram try to keep approximately equal across buckets?
options: Domain width
The number of table pages used by each row
B+ tree height
The number of tuples in each bucket
questions.explanation: Equi-width keeps interval width equal. Equi-depth instead aims for equal tuple counts, or depths.

questions.prompt: A table has 120 rows divided into 4 ideal equi-depth buckets. What is each bucket's depth?
questions.explanation: 120 / 4 = 30 rows per ideal bucket. The value 4 counts buckets, while 120 counts the whole table rather than one bucket.

questions.prompt: An equi-depth bucket over integer values [11,13] contains 30 rows. Assuming uniformity within it, how many rows are estimated for equality to 12?
questions.explanation: There are three possible values, so 30/3=10. Other buckets may have different widths without changing this calculation.

questions.prompt: Buckets [1,3] and [4,9] each contain 30 rows. Assuming uniformity within buckets, how many rows are estimated for A>6?
options: 45 rows
10 rows
15 rows
30 rows
questions.explanation: Values 7,8,9 occupy 3/6 of the second bucket, giving 15 rows. Taking the entire bucket would overestimate the result.

questions.prompt: Why does equi-depth adapt to dense regions of the data?
options: It uses equal-width intervals regardless of frequency
It removes hot values to make every bucket look uniform
It guarantees accurate correlations between all columns
It uses narrower intervals to keep each bucket's row count approximately equal
questions.explanation: Resolution is concentrated where more rows occur. A single-column histogram still cannot describe every correlation between columns.

questions.prompt: Three equi-depth integer buckets [1,3], [4,9], [10,12] contain 30 rows each. Assuming uniformity inside each bucket, how many rows satisfy A>=7?
questions.explanation: Values 7,8,9 retain half of the second bucket (15); all 30 rows in the last bucket remain. Total:45.
